title: H.M. and the hippocampus
text:
CHAPTER 9. MEMORY
SECTION 9.1. H.M. AND THE HIPPOCAMPUS

Where are memories stored?

For much of the first half of the twentieth century, the dominant view among experimental psychologists was that memory is not localized in any particular brain structure. Karl Lashley spent decades training rats on maze tasks and then removing different parts of their cortex, searching for the "engram," the physical trace of a memory. In a famous 1950 paper titled "In search of the engram," he concluded, half in jest, that his experiments seemed to show that learning was simply not possible, and more seriously, that memory traces are distributed widely across the cortex, with performance depending on the amount of cortex removed rather than its location. This fit Flourens's earlier view of equipotentiality (section 3.1).

The case that changed this view came not from an animal experiment but from a human patient, and from a surgical operation with tragic consequences.

Henry Molaison

Henry Gustav Molaison (1926 to 2008) was known to science for more than fifty years only by his initials, H.M., to protect his privacy. His full name was made public after his death in December 2008. He grew up in Connecticut in the United States. He began having seizures in childhood, possibly following a bicycle accident around the age of seven or nine (accounts differ), though a family history of epilepsy has also been noted. By his twenties, his epilepsy had become severe, with frequent major seizures despite high doses of anticonvulsant drugs, making it impossible for him to work or live a normal life.

In 1953, when H.M. was 27, the neurosurgeon William Beecher Scoville operated on him at Hartford Hospital in an attempt to control his seizures. Scoville removed tissue from the medial (inner) part of both temporal lobes, including much of the hippocampus, the amygdala, and the surrounding entorhinal and parahippocampal cortex, on both sides. Removing these structures on both sides was an experimental procedure. Scoville had performed similar operations on psychiatric patients, and the seizures appeared to originate in this region.

The operation reduced H.M.'s seizures considerably. But it had an unexpected and devastating side effect: H.M. could no longer form new lasting memories of events and facts. He lived the rest of his life, more than five decades, largely in the present moment.

Brenda Milner's studies

The psychologist Brenda Milner (born 1918), working at the Montreal Neurological Institute with Wilder Penfield, had studied patients who had undergone removal of one temporal lobe for epilepsy. Two of Penfield's patients had developed severe memory problems after a unilateral operation, which Penfield and Milner suspected was because the other hippocampus was already damaged. When Scoville learned of these cases, he contacted Penfield and Milner about H.M. Milner traveled to Hartford to study him.

In 1957, Scoville and Milner published a paper in the Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry titled "Loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions." It described H.M. along with several of Scoville's psychiatric patients who had undergone similar operations. The paper showed that bilateral removal of the medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampus, produced severe memory impairment, while removal of other temporal structures (such as the uncus and amygdala alone) did not. This paper is one of the most cited in neuroscience, and it marked the beginning of the modern study of memory systems.

What H.M. could and could not do

Over the following decades, Milner, and later Suzanne Corkin at MIT and many other researchers, studied H.M. in great detail. He was a willing and good-humored participant. Their findings revealed a remarkably specific pattern.

What was impaired:

- Anterograde amnesia. H.M. could not form new long-term memories of events (episodic memory) or new facts (semantic memory). He could not remember people he had met after the surgery, even if he had met them many times. He did not know where he lived after his family moved, could not keep track of current events, and would read the same magazine repeatedly without recognizing it. Researchers who worked with him for decades had to introduce themselves each time.
- Some retrograde amnesia. His memory for events in the years before his surgery was also impaired, particularly for the period of about a decade before the operation, though estimates of the extent changed with later testing. Corkin's later work suggested that his autobiographical memories from before the surgery were less detailed and less "relived" than normal, even for older periods.

What was preserved:

- Short-term (working) memory. H.M. could hold a small amount of information in mind for a short time, for example repeating a string of digits immediately, as long as he was not distracted. If he rehearsed continuously, he could keep a number in mind for many minutes. But once his attention shifted, the information was lost.
- Intelligence and language. His IQ was normal or slightly above average after the surgery, and his language and reasoning were largely intact.
- Older memories. He remembered much of his childhood and could recall many general facts learned before the surgery.
- Motor skill learning. In a famous experiment, Milner taught H.M. a mirror-drawing task: tracing the outline of a star while seeing his hand and the star only in a mirror, which reverses the movements and makes the task difficult at first. Over three days of practice, H.M. improved steadily, just like normal subjects. Yet each day he had no memory of having done the task before. He learned the skill without remembering learning it.
- Perceptual and other forms of implicit learning. Later studies showed that H.M. could show priming effects (improved processing of previously seen items) and could learn some other perceptual skills.

The dissociations and their meaning

H.M.'s case established several fundamental principles about memory, which shaped the field for decades.

1. Memory is a distinct brain function. H.M.'s memory impairment occurred against a background of normal intelligence, perception, and language. So memory can be separated from other cognitive abilities; it depends on specific brain structures.

2. The medial temporal lobe, and especially the hippocampus and surrounding cortex, is essential for forming new long-term memories of facts and events. Later research in animals and other patients refined the anatomy. A crucial case was patient R.B., studied by Larry Squire, Stuart Zola-Morgan, and David Amaral and reported in 1986: after an episode of reduced blood flow to the brain, R.B. developed significant anterograde amnesia, and after his death, careful examination of his brain showed damage restricted mainly to the CA1 field of the hippocampus on both sides. This showed that damage to the hippocampus alone is sufficient to produce amnesia (though R.B.'s amnesia was milder than H.M.'s, consistent with the additional damage in H.M. to surrounding cortex).

3. Short-term memory and long-term memory are different systems. H.M. had intact short-term memory but could not convert it into long-term memory. This supported the distinction between a temporary store and a permanent store, which had been proposed by psychologists such as William James (primary and secondary memory) and was formalized in models like that of Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin (1968).

4. The hippocampus is not the permanent storage site of all memories. Because H.M. retained many memories from long before his surgery, the hippocampus could not be the final storehouse of those memories. Instead, it seemed to be needed for forming new memories and for a period after they were formed, after which memories became independent of it. This idea, called systems consolidation, is the subject of section 9.2.

5. There are multiple memory systems. The mirror-drawing result showed that some forms of learning, such as motor skills, do not depend on the medial temporal lobe. This led to the distinction between declarative memory (memory for facts and events that can be consciously recalled, which requires the medial temporal lobe) and nondeclarative or procedural memory (skills, habits, priming, and conditioning, which depend on other brain structures such as the basal ganglia, cerebellum, and neocortex). Larry Squire and others developed this taxonomy in the 1980s.

The ethical dimension

H.M.'s operation was never repeated once its consequences were understood. Scoville himself warned against bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in the 1957 paper. Modern epilepsy surgery, when it removes temporal lobe tissue, does so on one side only, after careful testing to make sure that the remaining hemisphere can support memory. The story of H.M. thus combines a medical tragedy with an enormous scientific contribution. H.M. could not consent to research in the way we would expect today; his participation over many decades was arranged with the involvement of his family and later a court-appointed guardian. Researchers who knew him described his patience and warmth. The way his case was managed, including the control of access to him and the handling of his brain and data after his death, has been discussed in books and articles, including Luke Dittrich's 2016 book Patient H.M., which raised questions about the original surgery and about aspects of the research; some of its claims were disputed by researchers involved.

H.M.'s brain after death

H.M. agreed during his life (with his guardian's consent) to donate his brain for research. After his death in 2008, his brain was scanned with MRI, preserved, and then cut into thousands of very thin sections at the University of California, San Diego, by a team led by Jacopo Annese, in a process that was streamed live online in 2009. The resulting digital atlas, described in a 2014 paper in Nature Communications, allowed researchers to see exactly what had been removed and what remained. It showed that some posterior hippocampal tissue remained but was likely nonfunctional because its inputs from the entorhinal cortex had been removed, and it revealed a small lesion in the left orbitofrontal cortex, possibly caused during the surgery.

The hippocampus: anatomy

The hippocampus, named for its resemblance to a seahorse (Greek hippokampos) by the anatomist Giulio Cesare Aranzi in the sixteenth century, is a curved structure in the medial temporal lobe. Its basic circuit, which Cajal and his student Rafael Lorente de No described in detail, is often summarized as the "trisynaptic circuit":

1. Input arrives from the entorhinal cortex, which receives information from many areas of the neocortex, via the perforant path, to the granule cells of the dentate gyrus.
2. Dentate granule cells send their axons (mossy fibers) to pyramidal cells in the CA3 region.
3. CA3 pyramidal cells send axons (Schaffer collaterals) to pyramidal cells in CA1. CA3 cells also connect extensively with each other (recurrent collaterals).
4. CA1 sends output to the subiculum and back to the entorhinal cortex, and from there to the neocortex.

(There is also a direct pathway from entorhinal cortex to CA1 and CA3.) CA stands for cornu Ammonis, "horn of Ammon," an old name referring to the curved shape.

This anatomy suggests a functional loop: the hippocampus receives highly processed information from across the neocortex, processes it in a series of stages, and sends results back to the neocortex. The recurrent connections in CA3 caught the attention of theorists, because a network of neurons with recurrent excitatory connections modifiable by Hebbian learning can act as an autoassociative memory: it can store patterns and recall a complete pattern from a partial cue. David Marr proposed this in his 1971 theory of the hippocampus ("Simple memory: a theory for archicortex"), and Edmund Rolls, Bruce McNaughton, Richard Morris, and others developed it further. In such theories, the dentate gyrus performs "pattern separation," making similar inputs more distinct before they are stored (to reduce interference), and CA3 performs "pattern completion," retrieving whole memories from partial cues. These ideas have received experimental support from recordings and from studies in genetically modified mice, although the details remain debated.

The hippocampus is also one of the few places in the adult mammalian brain where new neurons are born (in the dentate gyrus), at least in rodents; whether and how much this happens in adult humans is a matter of active debate, discussed in section 11.2.

Bridge to AI: two kinds of learning

H.M.'s case reveals a division that is directly relevant to AI. H.M. could learn slowly through repetition (motor skills), but he could not learn quickly from a single experience (remembering an event or a new fact after encountering it once). The brain seems to have at least two learning systems: a fast system in the hippocampus that can store individual experiences after a single exposure, and slow systems in the neocortex and elsewhere that gradually extract regularities from many experiences.

Standard deep learning resembles the slow system. A neural network trained with gradient descent learns by making small changes to its weights over many examples. It is poor at learning from a single example; if you train it intensively on one new fact, it tends to overwrite older knowledge (catastrophic forgetting, discussed in section 11.3). In a sense, a standard neural network after training is like H.M.: it retains what it learned in the past, and it can perform skills, but it cannot form new lasting memories during use, unless it is retrained.

Large language models illustrate this vividly. During training, they absorb an enormous amount of information. After training, their weights are fixed. Within a conversation, they can use information provided in their context window, which works like a short-term or working memory: it is available while it is present but disappears when the conversation ends, much as H.M. could hold information while attending to it but lost it when distracted. To give such systems something like long-term memory for new information, engineers add external memory: databases that store past interactions or documents and retrieve relevant items when needed (retrieval-augmented generation). This is a rough engineering analog of a hippocampus: a fast, separate store that holds specific items and feeds them back to the slow-learning system.

We will develop this comparison further in section 9.4, after discussing systems consolidation and the hippocampus's role in spatial memory.

Summary

- Karl Lashley's search for the engram suggested memory is distributed, but the case of H.M. showed specific structures are crucial.
- Henry Molaison (H.M.) underwent bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in 1953 to treat severe epilepsy and developed profound anterograde amnesia.
- Scoville and Milner (1957) linked his amnesia to bilateral hippocampal damage; H.M. retained short-term memory, intelligence, older memories, and the ability to learn motor skills such as mirror drawing.
- His case established that memory is a distinct function, that the medial temporal lobe is necessary for forming new declarative memories, that short-term and long-term memory differ, that older memories become hippocampus-independent, and that there are multiple memory systems.
- The hippocampal circuit (dentate gyrus, CA3 with recurrent connections, CA1) inspired theories of pattern separation and pattern completion.
- Fast hippocampal and slow neocortical learning parallel the difference between external memory and weight-based learning in AI, and the context window of language models resembles working memory.
